title: Software Development
summary: Build the applications, websites, and systems that people use every day.
description: Software developers design, build, test, and maintain the programs and systems that power everything from mobile apps to enterprise platforms. It's one of the most flexible entry points into tech — the work ranges from front-end interfaces to back-end infrastructure.
responsibilities: Write and test code across the stack
Debug and fix issues in existing systems
Collaborate with designers and product teams
Review code and ship features incrementally
dayInLife: Most days are a mix of writing code, reviewing pull requests, and syncing with your team on what to build next. Expect a daily standup, a few hours of focused coding, and the occasional debugging rabbit hole.

title: Data Analytics
summary: Turn raw numbers into decisions — find the pattern, tell the story.
description: Data analysts collect, clean, and interpret data to help organizations make decisions. It's one of the most accessible tech-adjacent paths for people coming from a non-technical background.
dayInLife: You'll spend your morning pulling data and cleaning messy spreadsheets, then the afternoon building or updating dashboards and explaining what the numbers mean to people who don't work with data every day.

title: Cybersecurity
summary: Defend systems and data against the people trying to break them.
education: Certifications matter more than a degree here
description: Cybersecurity professionals protect networks, systems, and data from unauthorized access and attacks. Demand consistently outpaces supply, making it one of the more resilient tech career paths.
responsibilities: Monitor systems for threats and breaches
Maintain security policies and access controls
dayInLife: Expect to start by checking overnight security alerts, then split your time between monitoring systems, patching vulnerabilities, and occasionally responding to an active incident that needs immediate attention.

title: Cloud Computing
summary: Design and run the infrastructure that modern software depends on.
description: Cloud engineers design, deploy, and manage infrastructure on platforms like AWS, Azure, and GCP. As companies move off physical servers, this skill set has become one of the highest-paid entry paths in tech.
dayInLife: A typical day involves provisioning or troubleshooting cloud infrastructure, writing automation scripts, and keeping an eye on cost and performance dashboards across your team's services.

title: UI/UX Design
summary: Shape how a product looks, feels, and works for the person using it.
education: Portfolio matters more than a degree
description: UI/UX designers research how people use a product and design interfaces that are clear, usable, and pleasant. A strong portfolio of case studies is the main thing that gets you hired.
dayInLife: You'll move between research (talking to users or reviewing feedback), designing in Figma, and presenting your work to developers and stakeholders for feedback before it gets built.

title: Artificial Intelligence
summary: Build systems that learn from data instead of being explicitly programmed.
education: Math-heavy; a degree helps but isn't mandatory
description: AI and machine learning practitioners build models that recognize patterns and make predictions from data. It's one of the fastest-growing and most competitive fields, and generally expects stronger math fundamentals than other paths on this list.
dayInLife: Much of the day goes into preparing data, training and evaluating models, and reading about new techniques, with regular syncs to translate results into something the rest of the team can use.

title: DevOps Engineering
summary: Connect development and operations so software ships fast and stays stable.
education: Usually a step up from software development or cloud roles
description: DevOps engineers build and maintain the pipelines and infrastructure that let teams deploy software quickly and reliably. It blends software development with systems administration.
dayInLife: You're often the person keeping deployments smooth: writing pipeline scripts, responding to alerts, and automating away the manual steps that used to eat up everyone's time.

title: Data Science
summary: Go beyond dashboards to build predictive models from data.
education: Bachelor's helpful; strong math and stats expected
description: Data scientists go a step further than analysts — building predictive models, running experiments, and answering harder "what will happen next" questions rather than just "what happened."
responsibilities: Partner with engineering to productionize models
dayInLife: Expect a mix of exploratory analysis, model-building, and communicating uncertain results clearly to people who want a simple yes-or-no answer.

title: Mobile App Development
summary: Build the apps people carry in their pocket.
description: Mobile developers build native or cross-platform apps for iOS and Android. It's a strong path for people who want tight feedback loops and visible, tangible results from their work.
responsibilities: Build and maintain mobile app features
Publish and maintain app store listings
dayInLife: You'll build and test features on real devices, fix platform-specific bugs, and coordinate closely with design to make sure the app feels right, not just works.

title: Product Management
summary: Decide what gets built and why, and keep everyone rowing the same direction.
education: Rarely an entry-level role; usually a transition from another field
description: Product managers sit between users, business goals, and engineering, deciding what a team should build next and why. It's typically not a first tech job — most PMs transition in from engineering, design, or business roles.
responsibilities: Talk to users and analyze feedback
Track metrics and iterate on the roadmap
dayInLife: Your day is mostly meetings and messages: aligning engineering and design, talking to users, and constantly re-prioritizing what matters most this week.

title: QA Engineering
summary: Catch what breaks before your users do — build the tests that keep software honest.
description: QA engineers design and run the tests that catch bugs before they reach users — from manual exploratory testing to automated test suites that run on every code change. It's a strong entry point into software teams for people who think in edge cases and “what if a user does this instead.”
responsibilities: Write and maintain automated test suites
Perform manual and exploratory testing on new features
Track, reproduce, and document bugs for developers
Integrate testing into the CI/CD pipeline

roadmap.step: CI/CD basics for automated test runs

dayInLife: Expect a mix of running automated test suites, digging into a flaky test that fails intermittently, writing up a bug report with clear repro steps, and syncing with developers on whether something is a real bug or expected behavior.

title: Data Engineering
summary: Build the pipelines that get clean data where it needs to go, reliably.
education: Bachelor's in CS or related field preferred
description: Data engineers build and maintain the infrastructure that moves and transforms data — the pipelines that data analysts and scientists depend on to do their jobs. It's a more infrastructure-heavy path than analytics, closer to software engineering with a data focus.
responsibilities: Design and build ETL/ELT data pipelines
Maintain data warehouses and ensure data quality
Optimize queries and pipeline performance at scale
Partner with analysts and data scientists on data needs

roadmap.step: Build a portfolio pipeline project + apply

dayInLife: A typical day involves checking that overnight pipelines ran cleanly, debugging a data quality issue someone flagged, and working on a new pipeline to bring in a data source a team has been asking for.

title: Security Operations Analyst
summary: Watch the systems, catch the alerts, and respond before a small issue becomes a breach.
education: Bachelor's preferred, certifications carry real weight
description: Security operations (SOC) analysts monitor an organization's systems for threats in real time, triage alerts, and respond to incidents as they happen. It's often the most accessible entry point into cybersecurity, with a clear path toward more specialized security roles.
responsibilities: Monitor security alerts and dashboards for threats
Escalate and help coordinate incident response
Document findings and update detection rules
dayInLife: Shifts often start with a review of overnight alerts, followed by triaging anything that looks unusual, working a ticket through to resolution, and documenting what happened so the next analyst has context.

title: IT Support / Systems Administration
summary: Keep the hardware, accounts, and systems running so everyone else can do their jobs.
education: High school diploma + certification, often enough to start
description: IT support and systems administration is often the most accessible entry point into tech — helping people with hardware and software issues, managing user accounts, and keeping everyday systems running. Many people use it as a launchpad into cloud, security, or DevOps roles.
responsibilities: Resolve hardware, software, and account issues via a ticketing system
Set up and maintain workstations and user accounts
Maintain basic network and server uptime
Document recurring issues and their fixes
dayInLife: Expect a queue of tickets ranging from password resets to a server that needs attention, some hands-on hardware setup, and the satisfaction of turning someone's frustrating morning into a five-minute fix.

title: UX Research
summary: Find out what users actually need, before anyone spends time building the wrong thing.
education: Bachelor's in psychology, HCI, or related field common
description: UX researchers study how people actually use a product — through interviews, usability tests, and surveys — and turn those findings into insights that shape design and product decisions. It's a research-first path for people who like asking why more than they like pushing pixels.
responsibilities: Plan and conduct user interviews and usability tests
Present research to design and product teams
dayInLife: Days vary between running back-to-back user interviews, digging through session recordings for patterns, and putting together a findings deck that will actually change what the team builds next.
